items.body:
The Conservatives are calling on the government to release the full details of the proposed U.S. trade offer that Canada rejected.

  • Trade War Coverage on CTVNews.ca

Party members say they support the government’s decision to reject the offer but are unclear about what was on the table.

On Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods, including some that fall within Canada’s free trade deal with the U.S. and Mexico.

Here’s how things unfolded:

‘In this together’: former Conservative deputy leader

A former Conservative cabinet minister says she hopes Prime Minister Mark Carney will brief opposition members on the proposed trade deal and next steps.

“Having other folks leak and talk to reporters, it’s not helpful,” Lisa Raitt, who is also a member of the advisory committee on Canada-U.S. economic relations, told CTV News Channel on Sunday.

She added that she hopes Carney will set up a briefing in response to the Conservative leader’s request.

“It’s openness that’s needed,” she said.

“They want to know what’s in the deal that isn’t a deal and they want to know what programs are going to go forward for Canadians who are unfairly impacted by the 50 per cent tariff.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca Journalist

Release U.S. trade offer details: Conservatives

Federal conservatives are calling on the government to release the full details of the trade offer from the United States that Canada rejected this week.

In a letter to Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, Canada-U.S. relations critic Shuvaloy Majumdar said while his party supports the government’s decision to reject the deal, Parliament is in the dark on what was on the table.

“If there was a draft text of any agreement that both governments have seen, please release it. The U.S. administration has seen it. Your government has seen it. Canadians deserve to see it,” Majumdar wrote.

A spokesperson for the Bloc Québécois wouldn’t say whether they support the calls for the government to detail what the Americans were offering.

But the party reiterated calls for a meeting between the “recognized” party leaders in the House of Commons to get a briefing on the situation.

Green Party Leader Elizabeth May also said the party leaders should be briefed, but stopped short of demanding the trade details be made public.

“I think we should have at least a Zoom call or Teams meeting as we used to do under the former prime minister to make sure that we are all updated,” May said.

‘Job loss is inevitable’: B.C. Chamber of Commerce reacts to Trump tariffs

The head of the B.C. Chamber of Commerce said job losses are “inevitable” and the future of small and medium businesses is in peril after U.S. President Donald Trump imposed punishing new tariffs on Canadian goods.

“I think this is par for the course. We’re back on the merry-go-round. We did the math and counted 15 changes over the last 21 months. So, I think we just continue to live in this world of uncertainty,” Jen Riley, the chamber of commerce’s president and CEO, told CTV News Sunday.

In Riley’s estimation, small and medium sized businesses in British Columbia are set to bear a disproportionate burden.

“The exports we have to the United States are now going to have a 50 per cent tariff. And a lot of those that are going to get hit are small and medium businesses—and that level of tariffs is generally not something they can absorb,” Riley said.

“So, we are very worried here in British Columbia that small and medium businesses are not going to be able to make it out of this.”

Lisa Steacy, CTVNewsVancouver.ca Journalist

Read the full story here.

Eastern Canadian premiers renew pleas to buy local

Premiers in Eastern Canada are once again calling on residents to buy local as Canada squares off against the United States in an escalating trade war.

“Every dollar spent on an Island or Canadian product supports the worker who made it, the farmer who grew it, the fisher who caught it, the producer who processed it and the business that put it on the shelf,” said Rob Lantz, premier of P.E.I., in a news release Sunday.

The U.S. tariffs have hit businesses and workers in New Brunswick, Premier Susan Holt said in a statement on Saturday. “Now, more than ever, we need to double down on buying local and supporting New Brunswick businesses and workers.”

The tariffs will affect about $7.7 billion of exports from Quebec, said Christine Frechette, the province’s premier. “To buy Quebec products is not an economic action, it is a nationalistic action. It’s an action of solidarity.”

Minnesota school faces $7K spike in price for mascot costume

Parents at a Minnesota school say they are rushing to get a Trojan-themed mascot across the Canada-U.S. border by the end of the week to avoid paying a higher price due to the tariffs.

Sarah Kallal said she and other community members had been inspired to procure a “professional-grade costume” for the school’s baseball team, in their hometown of Trojan

The community had raised $14,000 for the costume.

On Monday, Kallal said she got a call from the costume company that they had to pay an extra $7,000.

“Honestly, I kind of thought the dream died,” Kallal said. “I’m not going to absorb that cost and I’m certainly not going to go back to our community to say, ‘Oh, by the way, can I get seven more thousand dollars?’”

She was floored to learn that President Trump’s proposal to place a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian imports was to blame. She never expected that kind of economic policy to hit home so directly in a smaller community like New Prague.“

It brings awareness to how it’s not going to just affect corporations and government,” Kallal said.

Trade war ‘devastating’ for Canada: Trump admin

The Trump administration on Sunday warned that Canada would be “foolish” to think it could win a trade war with the United States.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told “Fox News Sunday” talk show that Prime Minister Carney will return to negotiations “very very quickly, because it’s going to be devastating for his country.”

“We’re great trading partners, right? But Canada gets the benefit of trading with the U.S. way more than the U.S. gets the benefit of trading with Canada,” he said on the show.

“To think that they’re going to go to war with Donald Trump and actually win that war with the U.S., I think it’s foolish on their part.”

U.S. customers ‘paying the full brunt’

President and Chief Executive Officer of the Aluminium Association of Canada Jean Simard expressed his concern for the future of the aluminium industry following the collapse of the trade talks between Canada and the United States.

To put things into perspective, he said Canada produces 3.3 million tonnes of aluminium per year of which 90 per cent is exported.

He added, “90 per cent of the exported product goes to the U.S.”

Simard said in the U.S., “customers are paying the full brunt of the tariffs,” paying $1500 to $2000 more per ton than what Europe pays for the same amount.

However, he noted not reaching a deal with the U.S. was not “a bad thing” as the talks had increasingly shifted toward a “U.S.-based advantage to the detriment of Canada.”

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca Journalist

U.S. after ‘fortress North America’

International trade lawyer at Mccarthy Tétrault Ljiljana Stanić says the collapse of the tariff talks with the U.S. was “unexpected”.

“I think most people expected another extension was forthcoming,” she told CTV News Channel on Sunday.

On the issue of U.S. asking Canada to match Washington’s tariffs on other countries Stanić said, “it seemed like the United States was trying to build fortress North America.”

The trade lawyer said she believes “that was a lot to ask from Canada without having free trade with the United States.”

Stanić also noted that “trade disputes are easy to start but difficult to contain,” and added that the situation is now at a tipping point where trade tensions between the two sides can quickly escalate.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca Journalist

Trump: Canada wants benefits of statehood

In his Truth Social Post, Trump also claimed that Canada has charged U.S. farmers “massive amounts of tariffs” for many years.

Canada only imposes high tariffs on U.S. dairy exports if they exceed quota amounts.

“In reality, however, the countries exporting products to Canada will not pay the high tariff because they will simply not export more than was negotiated in the trade agreement under which they have access,” states the Dairy Farmers of Canada, a national lobby representing Canadian dairy producers.

Trump’s comments come after Prime Minister Carney delivered his own address on the trade dispute in which he said Canada is at economic “war” with the U.S.

In Carney’s address, he said last-minute changes by the U.S. to the deal lead to a breakdown negotiations.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca Journalist

We want to hear from you

Are you worried about how tariffs might affect your work? Have trade disruptions already impacted your job?

Share your story by emailing us at dotcom@bellmedia.ca with your name, general location and phone number in case we want to follow up.

Your comments may be used in a CTV News story.

Canada ‘at war?’

Carney was asked: “Why does it feel like, today, Mark Carney is going to war, trade war?”

“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” he responded.

He said Canada had waited for the U.S. to implement tariffs to respond this way, and now that they have, “we’ve got the reserves. We’ve got the resilience”

“We’ve got the plan, we’ve got the focus,” he continued. “We’re going to focus on what we can control. We’re going to build.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

PM: Retaliatory tariffs to come after Labour Day

Carney said retaliatory tariffs, in response to Trump’s new levies, will come into force on Sept. 8.

In his address on Saturday, Carney acknowledged that the tariffs will “raise costs and reduce choice” for Canadians.

But at the same time, we take this step confident that it is in the best interest of Canada, and that by rejecting a bad deal by standing up for Canada, (we focus) on what we can control,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Kinew stands with Carney, vows to fight back

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says he fully supports Prime Minister Mark Carney and the federal government’s decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States.

Speaking Saturday afternoon, Kinew commended the prime minister for standing up for Canadians and that all premiers are united with Carney.

“History will not be kind to Donald Trump. So we should never appease him and we should fight back, which is what Canada is doing today,” said Kinew. “We can fight back against Donald Trump by buying from Canadian businesses, by supporting Canadian workers and most importantly, by living up to our Canadian values.”

Devon McKendrick, CTV News Winnipeg Editorial Producer

Read the full story here.

U.S. tariffs are violation of CUSMA deal, Sask. premier says

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe is calling new U.S. tariffs a violation of the CUSMA trade deal.

“Last minute changes by U.S. negotiators undermined the fairness and reliability of the deal,” Moe said in an X post on Saturday.

Moe says over the past few days, the Canadian government was working toward a deal that would have avoided new tariffs and reduced some tariffs that were previously imposed by the U.S.

“The new 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on some Canadian goods are a clear violation of CUSMA and a clear indication that the current U.S. administration cannot be trusted to live up to its own trade deals,” Moe’s statement read.

Caitlin Brezinski, Digital Journalist, CTV News Regina

Read the full story here

U.S. proposals would turn Canada into 51st state: Eby

B.C. Premier David Eby says a request from U.S. negotiators would have effectively reduced Canada to America’s 51st state.

“The suggestion that Canada would not trade with other countries or reduce our trade with other countries because the Americans tell us to would reduce us to the economic equivalent of the 51st state,” said Eby, fresh from a meeting with Carney, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and other premiers.

Earlier today, Carney was asked for specifics on what he called new and “economically unfair” terms proposed by American negotiators.

He said the U.S. had made efforts to “restrict our ability to have other trade deals” in the last hours of trade talks.

“The prime minister and his team rightly walked away from any suggestion that we would agree to that,” said Eby.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Read the full story here.

North ready to create jobs: NWT premier

The premier of Northwest Territories says the North is ready to create jobs, strengthen Canadian supply chains, open new markets and make Canada more self-reliant.

R.J. Simpson says Canada tried to negotiate with the U.S. government in good faith, and the prime minister was right to walk away from trade talks rather than accept a deal at any cost.

Simpson says Canada can build its economic strength at home and N.W.T. is a big part of the nation-building work that’s coming.

Canada after ‘win-win’ partnership

Executive Director of the Independent Wood Processors Association in B.C. Brian Menzies says he is “concerned” about the 50 per cent tariffs on the wood industry.

Speaking to CTV News Channel Saturday, he said companies will shortly have to make decisions about continuing their operations and keeping people employed.

Menzies said Canada is a country that wants a “win-win” relationship with its trade partners, adding that if our customers and partners in the United States don’t win, “we don’t win.”

He said Canada is on the “right track” by keeping that principle in mind, and that the wood industry must now transition to other markets and will need some help adjusting to that.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

Wine industry benefiting from tariffs a ‘myth’

President of Wine Growers Canada Dan Paszkowski says the tariff war is destroying markets that have taken the Canadian wine industry decades to make.

In an interview with CTV News Channel, he said Canada cannot “control what Washington does but we can strengthen the Canadian wine industry” through federal investment programs.

Paszkowski said that “would provide us with a lot of certainty.”

He noted that investment is especially important because in three to four weeks, wine growers will start harvesting for this year, but added there is currently no support for that.

Paszkowski highlighted that it would be helpful if provincial and federal officials made it easy for “Canadians to find Canadian wine.”

He also said the Canadian wine industry benefiting from the tariffs is a “myth.”

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

Mark Carney chairs first ministers’ meeting

The Prime Minister’s Office says Mark Carney met virtually with provincial and territorial premiers Saturday to discuss the suspension of trade negotiations with the United States.

The PMO says Carney outlined next steps to protect Canadian interests, including dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs that will take effect on the Tuesday after Labour Day, along with additional measures to support Canadian workers and businesses affected by U.S. tariffs.

Carney also emphasized the importance of a united “Team Canada” approach, with continued collaboration between the federal, provincial and territorial governments on nation-building projects, diversifying export markets and removing internal trade barriers.

Tammy Ibrahimpour, CTV News National Digital Producer

Canada avoided a ‘chokehold’

International trade analyst and government affairs specialist at Gowling WLG Jacques Shore says by walking away from the tariff talks, Canada has avoided a “chokehold.”

In an interview with CTV News Channel, Shore described the situation as a “missed opportunity” for the United States.

He said the last-minute conditions put forward in the talks by the U.S. were “surprising.”

Shore highlighted that it would be hard to imagine that “we would be restricted from engaging with other countries” and making decisions that are only Canada’s to make.

He said despite these “trade tensions,” Canada and the U.S. are integrated and will be working together.

Shore added that, at this point, there are “Americans who are scratching their heads wondering how this could have happened to Canada.”He said this will “harm the American economy,” but Canada alsohas to brace itself.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

F bombs in a trade war

California Governor Gavin Newsom made his feelings clear on social media Saturday morning.

“Our closest ally. Our critical trading partner. And Trump is hitting Canada with 50% tariffs,” wrote Newsom on X. “What the actual f--- are we doing?”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Deal would have not brought back auto jobs to Brampton: mayor

Patrick Brown, the mayor of Brampton, Ont., also commended the prime minister’s decision not to accept a bad deal and to match the new U.S. tariffs.

“This is not a trade war that we have asked for. Unfortunately, we’re in it because of the misguided policies of Donald Trump. But it doesn’t mean we should take it lying down,” Brown said in an interview with CP24 on Saturday afternoon.

“When I hear the premier and the prime minister say tariff for tariff, it’s our only recourse. We can’t continue to be bullied by this president.”

He noted that the reported terms of the deal that included permanent tariffs on the auto sector wouldn’t have brought the jobs at the Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant, which has been idling since 2023.

Last week, Unifor claimed that Stellantis was seriously considering closing and selling the plant.

“Stellantis made it clear to me that as long as there are tariffs, there was no business case for auto production in Canada, and they were leaving until tariffs were lifted. So, I’m glad the prime minister didn’t accept a bad deal,” Brown said.

“It would not have salvaged the auto sector in Canada.”

Bryann Aguilar, CP24.com/CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Uncertainty better than certainty around a bad deal’

President and CEO of Global Automakers of Canada Lucas Malinowski believes it’s “unfortunate” that the U.S. and Canada couldn’t come to an agreement regarding the auto industry.

In an interview with CTV News Channel, he said the North American auto sector has incurred $110 billion in tariff-related costs over the past year and a half, making the industry “less competitive” and cars “more expensive” for consumers.

Yet, he admitted that, at the end of the day, “uncertainty is still better than certainty around a bad deal.”

Malinowski also said the deal on the table was “untenable,” based on Prime Minister Carney’s remarks and what the government has said.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Two-year root canal’ ahead for Canadians, Sarnia mayor says

Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley says Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision regarding the tariff talks was “100 per cent” correct but admits “the tough stuff” will now start.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration will “search and destroy” every relationship it has around the world in the next two years, including ties with Canada, he said in an interview with CTV News Channel. “Canadians need to stand together.”

Bradley said the situation for Canadians will be like a “permanent root canal for the next year or two,” but added that “it will be worth it.”

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘There are no deals’ with Trump: Former Harper aide

Former Director of Communications to Stephen Harper Kory Teneycke believes Prime Minister Mark Carney should prepare the nation for an “incredibly difficult period of time,” but supports Canada’s approach in the tariff talks.

In an interview with Vassy Kapelos on CTV News Channel, he said that if there is one thing we’ve learned from U.S. President Donald Trump, it’s that “there are no deals.”

Teneycke described Trump as a president who “has broken every agreement he has made on every topic” since he took office.

“He is the kind of guy who starts bombing you when you’re in peace talks,” he said, adding that Canada didn’t start this war, but “we’re going to be there to finish it.”

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

No deal was ‘surprising’: trade lawyer

Greg Kanargelidis, an international trade lawyer, said not reaching an agreement with the U.S. over the tariffs was “surprising”.

In an interview with CTV News Channel on Saturday, he said, “it was surprising to hear… about talks collapsing.”He said Canadian importers will be impacted by tariffs, but they could, in part, be compensated for through remissions orders.

The trade lawyer added that the tariffs will also impact a wide range of goods, including agricultural products, wood products, electronics, sporting goods, dairy and alcohol.

He noted the impact for companies in those industries will be “perhaps impossible to withstand.”.

Kanargelidis said the discussions could also serve as a “base” for CUSMA negotiations but admitted they may be at a “standstill” for the time being.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump ‘can’t be trusted’: Ford

Ontario Premier Doug Ford criticized U.S. President Donald Trump, portraying him as an untrustworthy bully whose tariff strategy harms both Canadians and Americans.

He says Trump “can’t be trusted” because “he changes the deal” and “keeps moving the goalpost.”

Speaking to reporters, Ford added that Trump is “the type of person that would steal your lunch money the first day, he’d steal the toque off your head the second day, and the third day he’d steal your running shoes.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘No deal is better than a bad deal’: Ford told Carney in letter

In a newly released letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, Ontario Premier Doug Ford urged Ottawa to stand firm against the United States after President Donald Trump’s latest tariffs took effect following the collapse of last-minute trade talks.

The premier had largely remained quiet in recent days as negotiations continued.

However, in the letter, Ford told Carney that “no deal is better than a bad deal” that could encourage the United States to seek further concessions from Canada.

“We cannot allow arbitrary deadlines, shifting justifications or escalating tariff threats to weaken our resolve,” Ford wrote.

He said Ontario would not support removing its existing retaliatory measures without a deal that provides “significant relief” for Ontario workers, businesses and key sectors

Jermaine Wilson, CTVNews.ca Journalist

PM: U.S. proposed new ‘unfair’ terms

Carney said that progress was being made on negotiations towards a “mutually beneficial deal.” But in recent days, American negotiators proposed “new terms that were economically unfair.”

The terms “undermined net benefits for Canadians and called into question the reliability of any deal,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Last-minute changes

Carney was asked to specify what the U.S. sought to change in the final hours of negotiations.

Among those changes, he said the Americans had proposed a treatment of auto trade that was unacceptable to the Canadian team.

He also said the U.S. had taken “efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals,” and that “we believe in free trade.”

Carney was asked later if Canada had any of its own last-minute requests.

“’No’ is the short answer,” he responded.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Changes included auto, trade restrictions

The U.S. made “last-minute” requests to change the deal regarding the auto sector and Canada’s capacity to have other trade accords, according to Carney.

“The Americans wanted to limit it to autos only, not include medium and heavy duty trucks which is a big change, obviously,” he said.

Negotiators also introduced “at the last hour” efforts to restrict Canada’s ability to have other trade deals, he added.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Would Canada tariff other countries in co-ordination with U.S.?

When asked by a reporter if the U.S. expected Canada to tariff other countries as part of a trade deal, Carney responded, “there were elements of that.”

Canada could agree to that as part of an “integrated” market system with the U.S., Carney added.

But if that’s what the Americans are after, Carney said American tariffs on Canadian exports should be “clearly the lowest” among trading partners.

Asked why he thought the U.S. was interested in influencing Canadian foreign trade policy, Carney said “it’s a power play.”

Devika Desai and Luca Caruso-Moro,, CTVNews.ca journalist

B.C. Premier to address trade talks at 3 p.m. EDT

B.C. Premier David Eby will address the breakdown in trade talks in Vancouver at 3 p.m. EDT.

This follows the prime minister’s own remarks earlier today on the breakdown in negotiations between Canada and U.S. trade representatives shortly before the Trump’s tariff deadline expired.

In a social media post earlier today, Eby stated that “British Columbians will always stand with Canada.”

“We didn’t ask for this, but we’ll keep fighting for as long as it takes,” his post reads.

Follow along for more information here.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Mastering energy is mastering destiny’

Carney said Canada has been putting efforts towards ‘mastering energy’ and becoming an independent superpower.

“We’ve doubled the capacity of our electrical network from (now) to 2050,” he said.

He referred to an announcement made on Monday by federal government, Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, to update and expand the Churchills Falls generating station, as well as develop the Gull island project and transmissions.

He described it as the “single largest investment in Canada’s history to build the largest clean energy project.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

PM: Canada investing local

Canada will invest $25 billion to protect workers and businesses affected by the tariffs, Carney said.

This will include investments in “equipment, productivity and supply chain resilience,” as well as financing large companies to keep employers “afloat,” he added.

“We’re helping those hardest hit industries retool and pivot to those new international markets, and we’re being our own best customers,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

PM: Tariffs will hit U.S. steel and dairy

Carney said the retaliatory tariffs will hit sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agriculture, electronics.

“Also include products that are currently subject to unjustified Section 232 tariffs. This is a focused response to protect and defend our industries and allow them to compete with U.S. products in the Canadian market,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Premier pushback did not ‘factor’ in negotiations

Pushback from premiers in recent days over returning U.S. booze to stores did not factor into suspending trade negotiations, Carney said.

“The essence of (Wednesday’s meeting) was ... that we were on a path to a potential deal that would give Canadians ... the best deal in all our strategic sectors,” he said.

The price for that deal was “worth paying,” he added.

Last-minute changes by the Americans made the deal ‘uneconomic’, he added. “So we’re not asking the premiers to do anything.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Tariff protection for Canadians on its way

Carney said that tariff protection will be provided to business affected by the U.S. tariffs.

“Many of them are small, medium-sized businesses,” he said. “They’re in a wide range of industries spread across the country, concentrated (in) Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia.”

He did not say when the protections will be announced but added that it will be released “in a few days.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

items.body:
The head of the B.C. Chamber of Commerce said job losses are “inevitable” and the future of small and medium businesses is in peril after U.S. President Donald Trump imposed punishing new tariffs on Canadian goods.

The industry association was—like so many individuals and groups—watching anxiously as the clock counted down to the weekend deadline and Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from negotiations.

Jen Riley, the chamber of commerce’s president and CEO, told CTV News Sunday that the most-recent development in the trade war has been frustratingly familiar.

“I think this is par for the course. We’re back on the merry-go-round. We did the math and counted 15 changes over the last 21 months. So, I think we just continue to live in this world of uncertainty,” she said.

In Riley’s estimation, small and medium sized businesses in British Columbia are set to bear a disproportionate burden.

“The exports we have to the United States are now going to have a 50 per cent tariff. And a lot of those that are going to get hit are small and medium businesses—and that level of tariffs is generally not something they can absorb,” Riley said.

“So, we are very worried here in British Columbia that small and medium businesses are not going to be able to make it out of this.”

Riley noted the struggling softwood lumber industry has been a key concern—and that tariffs on so-called “value-added wood” products represent yet another blow.

“We are hearing that job loss is inevitable,” she said.

“Our forestry sector has already been hit with 45 per cent all-in tariffs on our softwood lumber. And now things like pulp, paper, and paper products, things like door frames, are hitting that 50 per cent tariff as well.”

Still, Riley said she doesn’t doubt Carney made the right move.

“Hearing that sovereignty was on the table, I certainly understand how we got to this point,” she said.

Moving forward, Riley hopes government plans to support people and businesses impacted will materialize and that work to become less reliant on the U.S. will continue apace.

With files from CTV News Vancouver’s Shannon Paterson

items.body:
The fallout from the collapse of trade talks between Canada and the United States is reverberating on both sides of the border, with U.S. President Donald Trump escalating his rhetoric while facing growing opposition to a broader trade war at home.

Trump weighed in on the failed negotiations with Canada for the first time overnight, taking to social media to criticize the Canadian government.

“Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!,” the president wrote.

“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!! President DJT”

The comments came as the trade dispute received prominent coverage on U.S. television networks Sunday, with ABC News framing the dispute as “Canada vs. the United States” and NBC’s Meet the Press asking how much more Americans can afford as trade talks fall apart.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also took a hard line against Canada.

“To think that they’re going to go to war with Donald Trump and actually win that war with he U.S. I think it’s foolish on their part,” he told Fox News Sunday.

But the president is facing pushback from some Americans, including former vice-president Mike Pence.

“I think the last thing we need right now as our economy is getting back on its feet is a trade war with Canada,” Pence told CNN’s State of The Union, on Sunday.

American business groups have also been raising concerns about further escalation, warning that tariffs could increase costs for consumers and urging both countries to return to the negotiating table.

CTV News U.S. political commentator Eric Ham said Trump’s support among the business community could be tested by the escalating dispute.

“Donald Trump cares about the business class. He cares about those billionaires,” Ham said. “They don’t want this and they’re speaking out.”

In Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised retaliatory measures, including dollar-for-dollar tariffs on U.S. goods.

Those measures are set to take effect Sept. 8, creating a potential window for negotiations to resume.

Former Liberal MP Ralph Goodale, who sits on the prime minister’s advisory council on Canada-U.S. economic relations, said the pause could give the American side an opportunity to reconsider its approach.

“There may be an opportunity in this pause for the American side to regroup and to become a bit more coherent,” Goodale said.

Polling conducted before the latest breakdown in talks suggested Carney has political room to continue pushing back against the Trump administration.

CTV News political commentator Scott Reid said the dispute could be a prolonged one.

“I think we’re in this for a while,” Reid said, adding that a meaningful agreement may require a change in the political calculations south of the border.

“I think we’re going to have to see real change on the American side, a weakened political position, a drive and a desire that it’s in their self interest to strike a deal before we get back to the table in any meaningful way,” he added.

Carney has yet to release the full list of Canadian goods that would face retaliatory tariffs.

Release U.S. trade offer details: Conservatives

Meanwhile, federal Conservatives are calling for more transparency from the government.

In a letter to Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, Conservative shadow minister for Canada-U.S. relations Shuvaloy Majumdar is asking the government to release the full details of the trade offer from the U.S. that Canada rejected.

“If there was a draft text of any agreement that both governments have seen, please release it. The U.S. administration has seen it. Your government has seen it. Canadians deserve to see it,” Majumdar wrote.

In an interview with CTV News Sunday, Majumdar said his party supports the prime minister’s decision to walk away from the deal, but said to “release the deal, let us see the facts for what they are.”

“Canadians are sick and tired of being used as a punching bag by President Trump and want to see the certainty of a good deal for this country a tariff free deal for this country, we want to support the government in accomplishing that,” he said.

-With files from the Canadian Press

items.title: Carney warned about economic coercion. Now Trump is testing the Canadian prime minister
items.description: Mark Carney drew international attention as Canada’s prime minister by warning that middle powers must resist economic coercion by more powerful countries. Now U.S. President Donald Trump is putting that warning to the test with sweeping new tariffs.

items.body:
TORONTO — Mark Carney drew international attention as Canada’s prime minister by warning that middle powers must resist economic coercion by more powerful countries. Now U.S. President Donald Trump is putting that warning to the test with sweeping new tariffs that could show how much economic pain Canada can absorb.

Tensions escalated late Friday when Canada walked away from negotiations after Carney concluded the United States was demanding too much in exchange for tariff relief. The U.S. imposed 50 per cent duties Saturday on about US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, and Carney announced dollar-for-dollar retaliation beginning Sept. 8.

“We’re going to hit back,” Carney said.

Carney is doing what many other American allies have so far avoided: risking economic pain rather than yielding to tariff pressure.

For Carney, the showdown is the clearest test yet of his argument that middle powers must stand up to economic pressure from great powers such as the United States and China, even when it comes at a cost. Canada’s response could show how countries navigate a world in which long-standing alliances offer less protection and economic ties themselves become sources of leverage.

It could also shape how Carney is viewed at home and abroad, and how other U.S. allies respond to the Republican U.S. president.

The trade dispute also has become a test of sovereignty.

Carney said Washington introduced language in the final hours of negotiations that would have restricted Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries. He said that demand was “unacceptable” and “a question of sovereignty.”

British Columbia Premier David Eby said accepting such a condition would have reduced Canada “to the economic equivalent of the 51st state” — a status Trump has mused about often.

Canada becomes a test case for the world Carney warned about

Carney’s message resonated in January when he addressed the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, as Europe braced for Trump’s threats over Greenland and new tariffs.

Carney said the international order was undergoing “a rupture, not a transition.” He argued that sovereignty would depend increasingly on a country’s ability to “withstand pressure” and warned that middle powers negotiating alone with great powers do so from weakness.

Trump responded a day later by stressing Canada’s dependence on the United States. “ Canada lives because of the United States,” he said. “Remember that, Mark, the next time you make your statements.”

The U.S. president has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st U.S. state and dismissed the allies’ border as artificial. On Sunday, Trump returned to that theme, writing on Truth Social that “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!” and accusing Canada of charging U.S. farmers “massive amounts” of tariffs for years. “No more!!!” he wrote.

Seven months since Davos, Canada has become a test case for the world Carney described.

“Our government understood, before many, that America would transform all its commercial relationships,” Carney said Saturday. He accused Washington of using “economic integration as a weapon” and said its “signature was written in pencil.”

The price of resistance and will Canada show the way?

Historian Robert Bothwell said Canada is uniquely vulnerable to U.S. pressure.

“No country is more exposed than Canada,” Bothwell said. “Other countries have to fear American misbehavior, but none as much as Canada.”

Bothwell said success ultimately means Canada retaining its independence “in the face of Trump’s desire to subordinate it and absorb it.” He said Carney “sees that very well.”

But Canada’s dependence on the U.S. market makes that difficult.

Nearly three-quarters of Canadian exports go to the United States, whose economy is roughly 10 times larger. Canada can sign new trade agreements, but replacing customers and supply chains built around the enormous U.S. market over decades is considerably harder.

Carney acknowledged retaliation would “raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer rejected Canada’s account of the breakdown in talks, saying Ottawa introduced new demands and backed away from commitments even after Washington offered to reduce tariffs on steel, autos, lumber and other goods.

He said the United States was moving ahead with additional measures in response to Canada’s retaliation, raising the prospect of further escalation.

The European Union prepared retaliatory tariffs against the United States last year but repeatedly suspended them while negotiating with Washington.

Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of Toronto, said Canada is providing the biggest test yet of whether Carney’s strategy can work and whether resistance by one middle power could change the calculations of others.

“Will there be a domino effect? We’ll see,” Wiseman said.

Carney’s defiance also drew notice in Europe. Former Italian Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni, who later served as the European Union’s economy commissioner, shared video of Carney’s Saturday remarks on social media and wrote, “Here is a speech I would like to hear in Europe.”

Carney tries to hold the line as anger grows among Canadians toward Trump

Ian Bremmer, president of the Eurasia Group, said Americans underestimate how angry Canadians are with the Trump administration.

“Taking a hard line in response to U.S. policy perceived as predatory — even with major economic cost to Canada — is popular among most Canadians,” he said in a social media post.

The confrontation is also reviving calls to shun U.S. goods. Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette urged residents to buy local, calling it “a nationalistic action” and “an action of solidarity.”

That anger again spilled into sports over the weekend. Fans in Vancouver and Montreal booed the U.S. national anthem before Major League Soccer matches Saturday, echoing similar scenes early in the trade war last year.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said Canadians should be prepared for a prolonged confrontation and that Trump could emerge weaker after the U.S. midterm elections in November.

“He’s got two more years left in office. We should be prepared to duke it out for two years, and then hopefully, sanity will return,” Kinew said.

Carney has framed the confrontation as a test of whether Canada can preserve its independence under U.S. pressure.

“Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so that they can own us,” Carney said Saturday. “And I promised: ‘That will never, ever happen.’ We are keeping that promise.”

items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Major media weigh in on Canada-U.S. trade tensions.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The collapse of Canada-U.S. tariff talks has drawn sharp attention from major international news organizations.
items.body:
The Canada-U.S. trade relationship has entered a new phase, and the fallout is being watched far beyond North America.

After negotiations between Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government and U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration collapsed late Friday, new 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian goods took effect. Carney has vowed to respond with tariffs of his own, setting the stage for a deeper confrontation between two countries whose economies are closely intertwined.

The reaction from major international news organizations reflects just how consequential the breakdown could become.

BBC focuses on Trump’s 51st-state rhetoric

The BBC’s coverage puts Trump’s longstanding suggestion that Canada could become the “51st state” near the centre of the story.

Its headline “Trump says Canada wants ‘benefits’ of being U.S. state after trade talks collapse” underscores the increasingly personal and political nature of the dispute.

The BBC reports that Trump accused Canada of wanting the advantages of being a U.S. state while avoiding the obligations, as Carney described the latest tariffs as a “miscalculation” intended to “hurt and divide us.”

The report also emphasizes the uncertainty surrounding the next steps, noting that the collapse has upended a deeply integrated trading relationship with no clear path to a resolution.

The Guardian highlights a trade war

The Guardian takes a more confrontational approach, framing the dispute as a full-blown trade war.

Its headline, “‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade war,” emphasizes Trump’s angry response and the escalation in tariffs.

The Guardian also focuses on the symbolism of the new duties, noting they impact an assortment of Canadian goods, from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.

Like the BBC, it points to the potential threat to the Canada–United States–Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), suggesting the dispute could extend well beyond the immediate tariff fight.

New York Times analysis focuses on Carney’s gamble

The New York Times takes a different angle in an analysis, centring its coverage on Carney’s decision to walk away from what he considered an unacceptable deal.

Its headline, “Carney stands up to Trump in trade war despite the risks,” presents the prime minister’s position as both a political stand and a potentially costly gamble.

It notes that many Canadians support Carney’s approach, while warning that the economic consequences could be significant.

That framing puts the focus not only on the dispute itself, but also on the risks involved in Canada’s decision.

The Washington Post sees a setback for Trump’s strategy

The Washington Post takes a broader look at the implications for Trump’s trade policy.

Its headline, “U.S.-Canada breakdown shows limits of Trump’s aggressive trade strategy,” suggests the collapse could demonstrate the limits of using tariffs and pressure to force trading partners into agreements.

The Post also describes the breakdown as a setback and notes that other countries unhappy with their trade relationships with Washington could be watching how Canada responds.

CNN: Carney says U.S. asked ‘too much’

CNN focused on Prime Minister Mark Carney’s claim that Washington demanded too much while offering too little in the failed trade negotiations.

The report highlighted his pledge to impose “dollar-for-dollar” tariffs on about $28 billion worth of U.S. goods, covering products including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp, paper and electronics.

The story also laid out the competing positions.

Carney said the U.S. had proposed “uneconomic” and “unfair” terms, particularly around key industries such as autos.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, said Canada had walked away from an agreement that would have delivered major tariff reductions.

CNN also noted that the latest tariffs affect only about 5 per cent of U.S. imports from Canada, but warned the bigger concern is the renewed risk of a broader trade war between the two countries.

Fox News: Canada walked away from ‘the best deal’

Fox News framed the collapse through the U.S. administration’s position, highlighting U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer’s claim that Canada rejected “the best deal” Washington had offered.

Greer said the U.S. had been prepared to reduce tariffs on Canadian steel, autos and lumber, but accused Ottawa of choosing to preserve trade barriers against American goods. He said the administration’s focus was protecting U.S. workers and supply chains.

The report contrasted with Carney’s remarks that Washington had made unfair last-minute changes. It also highlighted Greer’s remarks that no new trade talks are currently scheduled, suggesting the dispute could remain unresolved as both countries move ahead with retaliatory measures.

items.body:
Premiers in Eastern Canada are once again calling on residents to buy local as Canada squares off against the United States in an escalating trade war.

Premiers in Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have urged residents to seek out products made in Canada and in their home provinces since U.S. President Donald Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports on Saturday.

“Every dollar spent on an Island or Canadian product supports the worker who made it, the farmer who grew it, the fisher who caught it, the producer who processed it and the business that put it on the shelf,” said Rob Lantz, premier of P.E.I., in a news release Sunday. “Where we spend our hard-earned money matters. Those choices add up.”

Premiers across Canada first beseeched people to buy local last year, when Trump was threatening 25 per cent tariffs on many Canadian goods. When trade talks broke off late Friday night between the two countries, Trump made good on his threat to introduce 50 per cent tariffs targeting Canadian goods ranging from hockey sticks and honey to essential oils and dairy products.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has fired back, vowing to retaliate dollar-for-dollar with levies on U.S. goods beginning next month. He said more details on those retaliatory measures, as well as supports for affected sectors, will be announced in coming days.

The U.S. tariffs have hit businesses and workers in New Brunswick, Premier Susan Holt said in a statement on Saturday.

“Now, more than ever, we need to double down on buying local and supporting New Brunswick businesses and workers,” she said.

The tariffs will affect about $7.7 billion of exports from Quebec, said Christine Fréchette, the province’s premier. If each family in the province bought $25 worth of local goods each week, the spinoff effects would inject about $3 billion back into the economy, she told reporters on Saturday.

“To buy Quebec products is not an economic action, it is a nationalistic action. It’s an action of solidarity,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 23, 2026.

items.body:
The Trump administration on Sunday warned that Canada would be “foolish” to think it could win a trade war with the United States, predicting a “devastating” impact on its northern neighbour.

Negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down late Friday, putting into force new 50-percent U.S. tariffs impacting about US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States.

Canada in retaliation said it would match U.S. tariffs, with new levies notably targeting the U.S. steel and dairy industries to take effect on September 8.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Canada would come out worse from tussling with President Donald Trump in a trade war.

The United States currently accounts for roughly 70 percent of Canadian exports.

“We’re great trading partners, right? But Canada gets the benefit of trading with the U.S. way more than the U.S. gets the benefit of trading with Canada,” he told the “Fox News Sunday” talk show.

“To think that they’re going to go to war with Donald Trump and actually win that war with the U.S., I think it’s foolish on their part.”

He predicted that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney would return to negotiations “very very quickly, because it’s going to be devastating for his country.”

Carney was defiant on Saturday, announcing retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. after walking away from a “bad deal” on trade as the rift between the longtime allies deepened.

“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said.

Carney cited last-minute U.S. demands that would restrict Canadian trade deals with other countries and unacceptable “threats” to the French language and Quebec culture.

Trump hit back early Sunday, saying, “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!”

“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” Trump added in a post on Truth Social.

‘Bully in Washington’

The acrimony underscored the deepening rift between the close allies since Trump began his second term in January 2025 -- including his repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state.

Carney has said bilateral relations have been forever changed, and that Canada must reduce its reliance on the United States. Despite the economic fallout, he has won political support at home for his willingness to stand up to Washington since taking office two months after Trump returned to the presidency.

“We have a bully in Washington,” Canadian retired teacher Stuart Edwards told AFP Saturday in Fort Erie, Ontario in the shadow of the Peace Bridge, a conduit for billions of dollars in annual trade with the United States.

“We’re not going to put up with it, Canada isn’t. We’ll fight back,” he said.

In the recent talks in Washington, Canada was seeking relief from Trump’s tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, which have battered the country’s economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.

The White House had alleged “discriminatory treatment” by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told the New York Times on Saturday that the U.S. had offered to reduce its tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos, as well as eliminate a recently imposed tariff on Canadian lumber.

Greer said those measures would have given Canada “the most preferential treatment of any trading partner,” according to the Times.

He also said no new talks were planned with Canadian negotiators.

items.title: Will businesses pass along the extra tariff costs to consumers? Here’s what experts say.
items.description: The head of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business says Canadian businesses that have been absorbing the additional costs of tariffs so far, but they won’t have much choice but to pass those extra expenses to the consumer now.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Canadian Federation of Independent Business President and CEO Dan Kelly. (CFIB)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The head of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business says Canadian businesses that have been absorbing the additional costs of tariffs so far, but they won’t have much choice but to pass those extra expenses to the consumer now.
items.body:
The constant hum of machinery fills the large cavernous production floor of the Ultra-Form Manufacturing plant in Toronto, where employees take raw steel and aluminum material that had just arrived from the U.S., use the machines to process them into car parts and then ship it back to the United States.

“All of this aluminum, this comes from the U.S.,” Gurdeep Matharu tells CTV News while pointing at stacks of long aluminum bars, then walking over to towers of stacked boxes. “Then these get shipped back to Ohio, and these ones are going to Michigan.”

For Matharu, who is the business development manager of the company, there was a lot on the line during the recent trade talks between the U.S. and Canada, with hopes that aluminum and steel tariffs could be reduced from 50 per cent down to 25 per cent. But instead, with the talks falling apart and Prime Minister Mark Carney promising dollar-for-dollar counter tariffs in September, the situation for his employer could now worsen than before.

“The news was pretty hard to digest because for the last two years, Canadian industries have been suffering too much -- and then on top of that, you hear news like that, the uncertainty is too much ,” said Matharu.

“The counter-tariffs are going to hit us the hardest, now we have to tackle that -- so there’s more uncertainty in the market,” he added. “They not only hit your incoming raw materials but they hit you when you sell the parts out.”

So far, the company says they’ve held back from passing along the additional tariffs costs to their customers, but he’s not sure how long that can last under the current situation.

“Just to keep the customers, we tell [them], ‘okay, it’s an import tariff but we’ll take care of you,’ we take the tariff on our side just so we can keep the business going on,” said Matharu. “But you can do that only so much.”

The company owner, Kacee Vasudeva, says the government assistance has been a huge help so far, providing some relief from tariffs paid on both their imports and exports, and now is eagerly awaiting when the next announcement of aid will come. On Saturday, Carney promised an announcement to help businesses “early next week.”

“People want to do business but they’re not sure about these tariffs because it changes every two months -- and they’re struggling,” said Vasudeva about his conversations with his American business partners. “Right now I’m telling my customers ‘I will take care of tariffs, whatever happens.’”

Passing the costs off to the consumer

The head of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business says Canadian businesses that have been absorbing the additional costs of tariffs so far, but they won’t have much choice but to pass those extra expenses to the consumer now.

“The two big impacts on average Canadians are going to be on their jobs and on their prices,” said Dan Kelly in an interview with CTV News Saturday. “Sadly, I think the price impact is going to be quite significant -- and sadly, it’s going to be fairly immediate because businesses don’t have the bandwidth they used to be able to absorb these costs for any length of time.”

Kelly said the new promise of equally hard-hitting counter-tariffs is likely to have a self-inflicting effect.

“If that’s the case, we’re talking about food, we’re talking about basic groceries and all sorts of other consumer products, not just large industrial supplies,” said Kelly. “So, the impact is going to be fairly swift, as many Canadian importers are going to have to pass those costs along to their consumers.”

But according to Jean Simard, president of the Aluminium Association of Canada, Canada’s economy may bend, but there’s a good chance it won’t break, with how resilient it has been over the past year-and-a-half -- also leaning on creating new trade relationships with other countries.

“We found out and I found out through time that markets have a lot of resilience built in,” Simard told CTV News via Zoom Saturday. “And this is with this is what unfolded under our eyes over the past year, but it’s still kept the prices very high, which means that the cars, the dishwashers, the goods that we purchase normally, are affected in an inflationary way,” he added.

“The goods are costing more and they will keep costing more in the future.”

For Keith Currie, the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, how much of the increased expenses related to the tariffs highly depends on how much aid Ottawa will be announcing for businesses next week.

“We don’t know what the long term effect of this is going to be,” Currie told CTV News Channel Saturday. “I think before we panic, we need to have [Canada’s] best interests at heart, but we are concerned for the long term benefit of the economy of the agrifood industry as a whole. We want to make sure those ranchers have those options to go to.”

As for the Canadian wood sector, there are also likely to be tough decisions related to layoffs or increasing the prices of their goods.

Businesses have to make decisions now, especially with this new 50 percent tax, whether to keep operating or whether to keep people employed, said Brian Menzies with the Independent Wood Processors Association in an interview with CTV News Channel Saturday.

“They’ll be making these decisions shortly here and it’s going to make it harder and harder for these companies to continue,” he added.

items._ogDesc: This week’s top stories include Canadian home prices hitting near record highs and BoC researchers warn that rate cuts reduce affordability.
items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Bank of Canada Research Warns Rate Cuts Can Worsen Housing Affordability

Bank of Canada (BoC) researchers studied the impact of rate cuts on housing. They found that rate cuts boost buying immediately, with demand rising for up to 24 months. New supply follows nearly two years later, responding to the increase in demand. That’s how rate cuts are supposed to work, creating excess demand to boost prices and thus inflation. The researchers conclude that lower rates don’t improve affordability, but do the opposite.

Canada’s “Record” Housing Correction? Prices Near Highs In Most Provinces

The Great Canadian housing crash has produced the largest correction in history. Despite the industry’s headline data, most of the country is seeing the exact opposite. The national index shows that home prices are down 21.3% (-$179.3k) from the peak, but that’s almost entirely due to B.C. and Ontario. Those are the only provinces to show major drops, but most provinces are within 3 points of record highs. Market stimulus isn’t restoring activity; it’s boosting prices to new highs in most provinces.

Canadians Turn To Consumer Credit As Mortgage Debt Slows

Households are still racking up debt, but mortgage debt is playing a smaller role. Total household debt climbed 0.6% to $3.29 trillion in June, up 4.3% from last year. The vast majority remains mortgage debt, which has grown 4.2% over the past year. Meanwhile, consumer credit climbed 4.8% over the same period, one of the highest rates in over 16 years. Studies show consumer credit tends to rise after a housing boom, as recent buyers tap credit. That’s most likely what’s happening here, as credit agencies also note a rise in “distress borrowing.”

Canadian Home Prices Just Made The Sharpest Monthly Drop This Year

The CREA Home Price Index (HPI) shows that the price of a typical home across the country fell sharply. Prices fell 0.6% (-$3.8k) to $661,800 in July, the sharpest monthly drop since December. Sales came in 5.2% lower than last year, while new listings fell 6.0% over the same period, firming conditions. However, with sales near record lows and new listings near highs, the impact has been limited.

Canadian Inflation Hits BoC Limit As Broad Price Pressures Accelerate

Canada’s primary measure of inflation accelerated to 3.0% y/y in July, driven by gasoline (+25.7% y/y). However, this isn’t just a gas story—5 of 8 major components in the CPI basket show acceleration in annual growth. Inflation pressures are broadening while headline CPI is already near the Bank of Canada’s upper tolerance band. That gives the central bank limited options when it comes to responding to any shock.

items.title: Marco Mendicino: Why Mark Carney made the right call to walk away from Washington
items.description: Former federal cabinet minister Marco Mendicino defends Prime Minister Mark Carney's decision to walk away from the Washington trade talks.

Right: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with reporters before boarding Air Force One, Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md., en route to South Carolina. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Former federal cabinet minister Marco Mendicino defends Prime Minister Mark Carney's decision to walk away from the Washington trade talks.
items.body:
Marco Mendicino is a former federal prosecutor, federal cabinet minister for immigration and public safety and chief of staff to Prime Minister Mark Carney. He is now senior counsel at Cassels, Brock & Blackwell LLP. He is a political analyst for CTV News and a columnist for CTVNews.ca.

At some point in every high-stakes trade negotiation, there comes a defining moment when the leader of a country must decide whether the objective is simply to reach an agreement, or to protect the national interest.

Prime Minister Mark Carney faced that crucial test and made the right choice, recalling his negotiating team from Washington, D.C. after crunch talks collapsed with its American counterparts. If there was ever a moment to draw a line in the sand, this was it.

That said, the consequences are real. The newly imposed fifty percent tariffs will place targeted Canadian businesses and workers under considerable duress. Ironically, they will have a boomerang impact on the other side of the border, even if the Trump administration refuses to accept this reality. Their near-ideological belief that tariffs are a panacea for all that ails America is running into cold, hard economic data. This should shake their faith. Likely, it will not.

Fortunately, the prime minister has dedicated his professional life to solving economic crises. In his most pivotal speech since Davos, Mr. Carney returned to the upper foyer of the West Block to address the nation. There, in a sober tone, with clinical logic, and channeled emotion, he explained the breakdown in negotiations, and where the country goes from here. With architectural precision, the prime minister’s speech did four things.

First, he drew a line in the sand.

For more than a year, President Trump has upended trade relations around the world, indiscriminately inflicting economic harm on friend and foe alike. In Canada, the imposition of higher tariffs hit the auto, steel, aluminum, and forestry sectors hardest, constituting a flagrant violation of CUSMA, our pre-existing trade agreement which the president himself had negotiated.

Nevertheless, Canadians came to the table in good faith to settle on the terms of a new economic partnership with the United States. After a series of fits and starts, the latest round of talks reached an impasse when the Americans shifted their position on a number of proposals that would continue to threaten our auto and cultural sectors, and attempted to constrain our sovereign right to trade with other countries. While citing these specific examples as unfair and uneconomic, the Prime Minister added that there was a cumulative dynamic that called into question whether any agreement could be relied upon at this time.

That was the crux of it. A deal “signed in pencil” is not a deal you can count on. It risks being a revocable transaction. However, the prime minister was not prepared to sacrifice on the altar of expedience key sectors of our economy, or our sovereignty.

Second, he mobilized the country for escalation.

The prime minister did not sugarcoat the escalation that would follow. Using his central banker “forward-guidance” format, Mr. Carney braced Canadians for more economic disruption, but committed further support for affected businesses and workers.

More striking was his candour about our own retaliation. The prime minister acknowledged plainly that dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs would likely raise costs for Canadians and narrow consumer choice while in force. Governments rarely make these admissions publicly. It would have been far more convenient to promise that the punishment runs in only one direction.

However, in these moments, Mr. Carney has demonstrated his preference to level with Canadians, and that is a source of his credibility. Rather than pretend this trade war will be free of cost, the prime minister readied the country for a fight that could result in some pain. Eyes wide open.

Third, he left the door open to getting back to the table.

Despite the turbulence ahead, the prime minister was explicit that Canada remains a good neighbour to the United States. As such, he believes that a resolution is still possible, subject to a number of important caveats. For starters, any agreement would have to be mutually beneficial, which is a guiding principle of any constructive trade relationship.

The agreed terms would need to restore and strengthen preferential access to our markets. A settlement would have to lower costs for workers and families on both sides of the border. It could not jeopardize our key industries and workers. And finally, a negotiated resolution could never impinge on Canadian sovereignty.

What else could impede the Americans getting back to the table, beyond what remains in dispute bilaterally? They have a lot on their plate, both internationally and domestically. The war in Iran. Inflation and cost-of-living pressures. The congressional midterms. Regarding the latter, it is not for us to comment on how Americans should decide their own elections. No matter who they choose to govern, we will work with them. All Canadians want is a good faith partner whose word holds.

Fourth, he put renewed discipline and focus behind Canada’s own economic agenda.

Rapidly accelerating the construction of major energy projects and critical infrastructure, like pipelines, mines, ports and transits. Re-industrializing the defence sector. Electrifying the country. Reducing internal trade barriers. Signing new trade agreements, as we diversify our exports abroad. These are the pillars of Mr. Carney’s economic agenda. Their installation has strengthened our fundamentals since he formed government. Follow-through to completion matters even more now.

There is one other point about the government’s agenda worth underscoring. Domestic capacity and trade diversification are not an emergency fallback after the talks with the U.S. collapsed. It was never Plan B. As Mr. Carney said, it has been Plan A since the day this government took office.

What comes next?

The prime minister laid down these markers throughout the course of his address. What comes next will determine whether the resoluteness with which it was delivered will translate into execution.

As the seasons turn, there are number of milestones to watch for on the horizon.

The upcoming cabinet and caucus retreats are the planning forums where the government sets the agenda ahead of Parliament’s return in the fall. Crucially, they offer the prime minister the chance to hear directly from his ministers and MPs, allowing him to keep his finger on the pulse of the people. Listening to their perspectives, along with partners at other levels in government, industry and stakeholders, can help to shape the government’s policy and narrative. Ongoing engagement will be instrumental in keeping unity across the country.

After this, the prime minister will convene Canada’s Investment Summit in Toronto. This signature event will attract the world’s wealthiest investors, who together manage over $100 trillion in assets — a staggering figure by any measure. They will find a Canadian economy that is more inviting of capital and opportunities to develop infrastructure and resources, yielding returns for investors.

  • More opinions and expert analyses

As summer turns to fall, and a new session of Parliament begins, this next phase will require even more strength, discipline and focus by the government. A tall task, but one they are up to.

The prime minister is using the bully pulpit in the moments that count. And it has never counted for him more than when he drew a line in the sand during these trade negotiations and said on behalf of the country: this is where we will stand.

items.description: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew fully supports Prime Minister Mark Carney and the federal government’s decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Wab Kinew speaking at the Manitoba legislature on Aug. 22, 2026. (Zachary Kitchen/CTV News Winnipeg)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew fully supports Prime Minister Mark Carney and the federal government’s decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States.
items.body:
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew fully supports Prime Minister Mark Carney and the federal government’s decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States.

Speaking Saturday afternoon, Kinew commended the prime minister for standing up for Canadians and that all premiers are united with Carney.

“History will not be kind to Donald Trump. So we should never appease him and we should fight back, which is what Canada is doing today,” said Kinew. “We can fight back against Donald Trump by buying from Canadian businesses, by supporting Canadian workers and most importantly, by living up to our Canadian values.”

Late Friday evening, both Canada and the U.S. announced a trade deal had fallen apart, which resulted in 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods from the States.

Carney has since announced reciprocal tariffs will come into effect next month.

The prime minister also mentioned that trade talks disintegrated after U.S. trade representatives tried to implement last-minute changes to the deal.

“Donald Trump has certainly changed the world, but he hasn’t changed us, and we also know that Donald Trump won’t be there forever. So let’s continue extending that hand of friendship to the American people, and hopefully they will have Donald Trump and his folks see the door very quickly and we could get back to better times with our neighbours to the south,” Kinew said.

Manitoba will continue to retaliate against the American tariffs, Kinew said, by ensuring U.S. booze stays off the shelves of liquor stores across the province, as well as moving away from American businesses who apply for any tenders in the province.

The premier is also figuring out next steps to help Manitoba industries that will be impacted.

“We’ll work together with the federal government to make sure that industries that are facing this uncertainty are going to get the necessary supports,” said Kinew.

“We’re fighting for you. Donald Trump wants to take away steel, he wants to take away manufacturing jobs from our country and we won’t let them. So we’re going to stand up for our country. We’re going to stand up because we know that the red maple leaf is stronger than that guy in the red hat down south.”

Kinew also had a message for Americans, saying their cost of living is going to continue to climb under these new tariffs.

“He continues to undermine any credibility that he has on the cost of living, and the worst part about it, even the MAGA-hat-wearing American crowd should realize, is that he doesn’t care,” he said. “He only cares about making his family richer.”

Gillingham doesn’t mince words on trade war

Winnipeg Mayor Scott Gillingham also commented on the trade war Saturday, saying there is only one group that is responsible for the latest dispute.

“It is the result of the President of the United States and his advisors continuing to follow through on his arrogant threat to try to control our country using ‘economic force,’” Gillingham said in a statement.

“I support free trade, but you can’t practice free trade when the leader of your biggest trading partner is trying to choke your economy into submission.”

Gillingham said the city will do whatever it can to help the provincial and federal governments “fight this bullying.”

The mayor is calling on all Canadians to join together and help each other prosper during this uncertain time.

items.title: Nearly 3 in 10 Canadian renters now rely on AI to find a home
items.description: Rentals.ca survey finds AI adoption now mainstream among active renters across the country
items.content: <p>Rentals.ca survey finds AI adoption now mainstream among active renters across the country</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639229390796970339.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rentals.ca survey finds AI adoption now mainstream among active renters across the country
items.body:
Nearly three in 10 Canadians actively searching for a rental are now using artificial intelligence tools to navigate that process, and most of them say it helps.

Rentals.ca's Spring 2026 Renter Preference Survey, conducted between May 5 and June 14, among 1,194 active renters across Canada, found that 28.5% of respondents had turned to AI tools such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini at some point during their apartment search.

Of those 340 users, 72.6% found the experience helpful. The 70.9% majority have yet to try AI-assisted searching, but at close to 30% adoption among active renters, the behaviour has moved well beyond early-adopter territory.

For mortgage brokers, the pattern is worth tracking. A significant share of today's renters are prospective first-time buyers, and the tools shaping how they research housing are likely to carry into how they approach financing decisions.

Brokers keeping pace with housing affordability trends and rental market conditions across Canada may increasingly encounter clients who arrive at the mortgage conversation already armed with AI-generated neighbourhood comparisons and affordability estimates.

What renters are doing with AI

Among the 340 respondents who reported using AI, applications spanned the full arc of the rental search process.

Finding listings or researching neighbourhoods was the most common use at 57.7%, followed by comparing rental prices across markets at 45.5%.

Understanding lease terms and provincial tenancy rules attracted 40.2% of users, an indication that renters are treating AI as an accessible, on-demand guide to legal complexity.

Getting budgeting and affordability advice accounted for 38.1%, while drafting messages to landlords drew 33.3%.

In a competitive market, applicants are using AI to present themselves more professionally. Discussions about how Canadians are navigating digital tools and payment security risks continue to grow, the degree to which AI-assisted content is entering the borrower funnel is a dynamic the industry will need to account for.

Who is and isn't adopting

The 25–34 cohort leads adoption at 35.5%, but the generational divide is narrower than the AI narrative would suggest. Renters aged 65 and over reported AI usage at 22.8%, nearly identical to the 45–54 cohort at 22.5%.

Income predicts uptake more sharply: those earning $125,000 or more adopt at 37.9%, compared to 23.8% among renters earning under $25,000, the group that arguably faces the most acute affordability pressure.

Regionally, Toronto and Ontario lead at 29.9%, while Québec and Montréal trail at 22.7%, a gap Rentals.ca attributes partly to the predominantly English-language nature of major AI platforms.

Across all other markets, adoption is broadly consistent, with fewer than 8 percentage points separating the highest and lowest regional figures.

Meanwhile, Canadians searching for homes in the country's more affordable markets are the most likely to encounter real estate listings written by AI, according to a study by Originality.ai. Human-written ads averaged $3,037 per month versus $2,997 for likely AI-generated ones.

Brokers advising buyers would do well to encourage clients to read listings critically, verify property details in person, and consult directly with realtors on any claims that seem unusually polished or unusually vague.
